articles.text: On Saturday, December 13, the typically quiet weekend campus of Piedmont Middle School was transformed into a bustling hub of engineering and high-energy competition. The Piedmont Makers held their annual FIRST LEGO League (FLL) Community Tournament, welcoming 350 kids across 55 teams to the league’s season finale. The energy on campus was palpable from the first moments of the day, in what turned out to be the largest tournament in the organization’s history. Over 750 attendees, comprising excited students, anxious coaches, supportive parents, and curious community members, packed the venue to witness the culmination of months of hard work. The air buzzed with the whir of Lego motors and the spirited cheers of teams rallying for their peers. “This event is the capstone of a huge amount of work done by these hard-working teams over the three months of this fall season,” said Shelley Rea, FLL Challenge Co-Commissioner for Piedmont Makers. “We celebrate all of them for their teamwork, innovative spirit, and engineering excellence!”

articles.text: Piedmont’s newest ambulance outside the station Piedmont has placed a newly outfitted ambulance into full service, marking a significant milestone for the city’s Fire Department and its emergency medical response capabilities. The ambulance arrived over the summer and spent several months being prepared for service before officially going into use in October. Piedmont is one of only four cities in Alameda County that provides its own ambulance transport, a distinction Fire Chief Dave Brannigan said has a direct impact on response times and patient care. “We have firefighters on the ambulance close by, and our response times are sub-three minutes, whereas in other parts of the county, it’s a private ambulance provider,” Brannigan said. “They’re trying to shave costs and afford to cover the whole county, so you can have much longer transport times if you live somewhere else.” Piedmont’s firefighter-paramedics work exclusively within the city, allowing for faster responses and continuity of care. articles.text: Piedmont’s Department of Public Works and first responders worked through the holidays to address the impacts of heavy rain across the city. On Christmas morning, Piedmont police officers and Public Works crews responded to a mudslide on Moraga Avenue that created a traffic hazard near the coaches’ field. The slide blocked the right lane, requiring officers to direct traffic while crews cleared the debris. Between December 23 and 26, Piedmont recorded 2.44 inches of rain. The storm caused localized flooding in several areas, including near the 7-Eleven and Exxon Mobil on Grand Avenue. Public Works crews cleared storm drains throughout the city to reduce flooding risks. High winds accompanied the rain, with gusts reaching up to 36 mph. The combination of wind and rain downed multiple trees, creating obstructions in local parks and along sidewalks. articles.text: Editor: I am writing with a friendly reminder to the community to watch out for deer and coyotes while on walks this time of year when there is less sunlight and vision can be impaired. I was on a walk-about in Upper Piedmont earlier this week reliving my “right-to-roam” trip through the Cotswolds in the UK and on more than one occasion I was spooked by a deer crashing through brush, across the road and into a neighbor’s yard. On another walk I was followed by a coyote for 5 minutes. The old redwoods in the hills near Hampton provide beautiful shading and light effects, but could also cause surprises with wildlife encounters. –Jay Bohanion
articles.title: Be on the lookout for deer, coyotes

articles.text: Every July 4 parade in Piedmont is led by Smokey Bear on a fire truck, reminding us that only you can prevent wildfires. That message once applied mostly to camping trips in the Sierra. Today, wildfire is a very real threat to Piedmont. The city took action this month to help ensure a future that is more resistant to wildfire. Now it is time for the rest of us to do our part. On Dec. 1, the Piedmont City Council designated all of Piedmont a Wildland Urban Interface (WUI) and adopted the state’s new WUI Fire Code. That decision matters. Stronger codes will steadily improve the safety of our housing stock over time. But adopting a code alone does not make us safer today. Replacing flammable siding and roofing materials makes us safer. Landscaping to keep vegetation away from structures makes us safer. Buildings constructed to the highest standards of fire resistance make us safer. The Piedmont Fire Department is here to help residents get started. Fire prevention experts are available to meet at your property to help identify potential improvements and develop a plan that fits Photos courtesy of the city Piedmont Fire Department Chief Dave Brannigan your time frame and resources. The new code sets a higher standard for future construction. But a more resilient community does not need to wait for “someday.” We can all make choices now to get there faster. Wildfire safety does not happen all at once. It is built step by step. Every Piedmont resident is encouraged to take the first step by learning, planning and making changes that make sense for their home and circumstances. You can contact the Piedmont Fire Department at 510-420-3030 to request an inspection. Ember-resistant zone example

articles.text: Blaze is a striking flame point Siamese mix with intense blue eyes and a big, engaging personality. While he may be shy at first, he quickly becomes confident, affectionate and eager to be part of the action, seeking out pets, playtime and companionship throughout the day. This smart, energetic cat thrives on interactive play and enrichment. Wand toys are a favorite, and daily play sessions help keep him happy and mentally engaged. articles.text: For many, the idea of speech therapy conjures images of children learning to pronounce sounds correctly or overcome stutters. However, speech therapy is not just for kids—it plays a crucial role in helping adults navigate communication challenges as well. Whether due to injury, illness, or long-standing speech difficulties, adults can benefit greatly from speech therapy. This vital healthcare service is often underutilized by adults who may not realize how much it can improve their quality of life. Speech therapy for adults is designed to help individuals improve their communication abilities. This may involve refining articulation, enhancing fluency, or strengthening the muscles used for speech. In adults, therapy is often necessary after medical events such as strokes, traumatic brain injuries or concussions, or surgeries. Speech-language pathologists (SLPs), or speech therapists, also work with adults experiencing conditions like Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), which can impact both speech and swallowing functions. Some adults may have dealt with speech issues throughout their lives, such as stuttering or voice disorders. Others may struggle newly acquired communication issues, such as aphasia, a condition that affects language comprehension and production, often following a stroke or brain injury. In these cases, speech therapy helps restore communication skills, empowering individuals to regain independence and confidence. Adults seek speech therapy for many reasons, but the primary goal is always the same: to improve communication and quality of life. For those recovering from strokes, speech therapy can help them regain the ability to speak clearly, which is critical for reestablishing social connections and functioning in everyday life. In some cases, therapy may involve relearning how to speak entirely. Similarly, individuals with degenerative neurological diseases, such as Parkinson’s, often face challenges with speech volume, clarity, and swallowing. Therapy can slow the progression of these issues, giving patients more control over their speech for longer periods. Voice disorders, caused by vocal strain, injury, or surgery, are another reason adults turn to speech therapists. Teachers, singers, and public speakers are especially prone to vocal damage and may require therapy to heal and retrain their vocal cords. Speech difficulties can be deeply frustrating, leading to feelings of isolation, embarrassment, and low self-esteem. Many adults find themselves withdrawing from social situations or avoiding conversations because they fear being misunderstood. The emotional toll can be as significant as the physical challenges. Speech therapy provides not only practical tools but emotional support. As patients make progress, their confidence grows. The ability to communicate effectively—whether in personal relationships, at work, or in public—can transform a person’s outlook on life. The therapeutic process is also about building a new identity around a stronger, more capable voice. For adults facing speech and communication challenges, speech therapy offers a lifeline. It’s more than just about words and sounds; it’s about reconnecting with the world. With the guidance of skilled speech-language pathologists, adults can overcome their speech limitations and rediscover the power of their voice. This journey may take time, but with persistence and expert help, the results can be life-changing. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language, reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com.

articles.text: The FIRST LEGO League competition is far more than playing with blocks. It is a multi-disciplinary challenge that asks students to engage in research, problem-solving, coding, and engineering. During the event, each of the 55 teams participated in four rounds of exciting robot match games. On the competition tables, autonomous robots— designed, built, and programmed entirely by the students—navigated complex missions to score points against a ticking clock. Off the field, teams were challenged by public speaking and a judged question and answer session. Every team faced a panel in a dedicated presentation pod. Here, they described their robot designs and showed off their Innovation Projects, which required them to identify a realworld problem and propose a unique solution. “It’s so much fun to see the creative solutions teams land on after talking with experts in the real world about their innovation projects,” said Ben Stein, co-president of Piedmont Makers. Stein noted that the depth of research conducted by these elementary and middle school students often rivals that of much older students. The sheer scale of the operation required a massive mobilization of community support. More than 100 volunteers dedicated their Saturday time to ensuring the event ran smoothly. This army of supporters included setup crews who transformed the gym, referees who kept close eyes on the robot tables, judges who evaluated presentations, and various tournament staff who managed the flow Team #71294, the “Glitter Bombs,” made friends with Makey the robot outside Buzz Redford Gym. Parents celebrated the teams during programmed robot runs. Only team members were allowed in the competition area.

It is a multi-disciplinary challenge that asks students to engage in research, problem-solving, coding, and engineering. On the competition tables, autonomous robots— designed, built, and programmed entirely by the students—navigated complex missions to score points against a ticking clock. articles.text: 5,300 miles away from everything you’ve known Math is a universal language until you’re sitting in class at a school halfway across the world wondering what is a surd. For all those wondering, a surd is an irrational number simplified in the form of a square root. This is just one of the growing pains you face when you decide you want to move to another country for school, after spending around nine years learning the intricacies of the American schooling system. Besides the relentless patronising of your accent, everyone is extremely welcoming and helpful, especially whilst navigating the absolute rabbit warren that is your school. I’m convinced the building genuinely has secret passages as I’ve frequently caught myself walking behind someone who turns into a strange corridor, only for her to reappear at my destination. Also, there appear to be around eight boys who have the same name, which you will be likely to mix up and face extreme embarrassment. Living in a boarding house with 40 other girls has been one of the most rewarding and secure experiences I’ve had. The knowledge of knowing that there’s always a friend around, someone to ask for advice or class notes. It feels less like a strictly controlled environment and more like a huge sleepover. The loving house parents foster a sense of camaraderie, helping us build lifelong connections with each other. While boarding provides a solid and welcoming community, the school’s relationship with the surrounding community is incredible, with constant fundraising for local charities. Recently, I volunteered at our biannual Evergreen Tea party, a school event which hosted local elderly community members for a holiday celebration. The event is completely supported and run by staff and students, which is an extremely rewarding experience. It’s truly fulfilling to be able to see the direct impact of our efforts and hear the stories of past school alumni. The odd thing is, you’ll find yourself less homesick than you thought. It’s not hard to become consumed by school, friends and extra activities. And while it’s a melancholy thought to look back upon, it’s somewhat comforting to know you find your home in the places you seek, with people there to welcome you.

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony closes its 2025–26 Symphonic Series with Fables & Folklore, a program centered on storytelling and cultural tradition, on Sunday, January 25 at the First Congregational Church of Berkeley. The concert begins at 4 p.m., marking the fourth and final performance of the Symphony’s 54th season series. Internationally acclaimed conductor Carolyn Kuan, music director of the Hartford Symphony Orchestra, will lead the program. “This program celebrates imagination and heritage, honoring cultural roots while inviting audiences to experience the power of storytelling through music,” said Executive Director Marion Atherton in a statement. The evening opens with Folk Songs for Orchestra by composer Huang Ruo. The work draws on traditional Chinese folk melodies, blending them with contemporary orchestral textures to evoke both personal memory and shared cultural history. Guitarist Marc Teicholz will Conductor Carolyn Kuan then join the Symphony for O Saci-Pererê, a guitar concerto by composer Clarice Assad inspired by Brazilian folklore. The piece centers on Saci, a mischievous trickster figure from Indigenous and Afro-Brazilian mythology, and features rhythmic energy and playful character alongside deeper reflections on Brazilian identity and oral tradition. Following intermission, the program concludes with Antonín Dvořák’s Symphony No. 8, a work rooted in the folk music of the Czech countryside. Known for its melodic richness and pastoral warmth, the symphony’s triumphant finale provides a celebratory close to the series. Single tickets are available at berkeleysymphony.org or by calling the box office at 510-841- 2800. All Symphonic Series concerts take place at the First Congregational Church of Berkeley.

articles.text: Shotgun Players extends its new production of Sunday in the Park with George, the Pulitzer Prize–winning musical by Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine, showing now through December 31 at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley. Directed by Susannah Martin with music direction by David Möschler, the show is inspired by Georges Seurat’s pointillist painting A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte. The musical explores the artist’s obsessive creative process and its impact on his relationships, and features immersive on-stage seating and an expanded bar menu. “This musical captures the questioning, fear, joy, and obsession that go into making art and the toll it takes on the people we love,” Director Susannah Martin said in a press release. “I’ve never experienced a musical which gets so deeply into the experience of being an artist and the process of making art.” “The sound-world of the show is just as daring, provocative, interesting, and non-traditional as the type of art that the character of George Seurat was striving to create,” added Möschler. “It’s not book scenes followed by songs belted out ad nauseum; it’s a score that is interwoven through dialogue and comes together more like a film score that helps create a strong sense of narrative and dramatic continuity from beginning to end.” Kevin Singer stars as George, with Marah Sotelo as Dot. The cast includes Alex Rodriguez, Laura Domingo, Jill Slyter and a 16-member ensemble. Artistic Director Patrick Dooley called the work a “legitimate masterpiece,” adding, “Sondheim captures the tension between artist and muse, beautifully and tragically.” Tickets and performance details are available at shotgunplayers.org. articles.text: Photo courtesy of The Exploratorium The children’s science museum becomes an adult playground every Thursday evening. Visit San Francisco’s Exploratorium every Thursday evening to experience the science museum “after hours.” After Dark is a recurring adults‑only event that transforms the museum into a late-night playground of science, art and sensory exploration from 6 to 10 p.m. Guests aged 18 and up are invited to wander through 700+ interactive exhibits focused on science, technology, engineering and more. With the lights dimmed, guests can explore the museum’s classic galleries, a live DJ set, themed programs and alcoholic and nonalcoholic drink options at cash bars. “It’s kind of like an adult playground,” Sam Sharkland, senior program developer at the Exploratorium, told ABC7. “It’s 18+, we have cocktails available and lots of extra programming, so you can almost be a kid or scratch that scientific curiosity that you may have lost.” Each Thursday features a different theme or special programming. Previous nights have included provocative films, talks tied to science and culture, live performances, and temporary exhibits. For more information, visit https://www.exploratorium. edu.

articles.text: The year 2025 is drawing to a close. The finish line is in sight. It reminds me of my days in high school when I was on the track team running the hurdles. To some they are obstacles, to others they are opportunities. Let’s look on the bright side. Sunday’s concert at St. Mary’s Cathedral in San Francisco was an inspiring memorial to the outstanding cellist Joel Cohen. Featured on the program were his friends and musical collaborators Wendy Loder, soprano, and Jeanette Wilkin Tietze, piano. The intimate concert in the gigantic space was a worthy memorial to Joel. Wendy Loder has a soprano voice of gentle quality which filled the large space easily. It seems that she has absolutely no vocal problems. In addition to her warm voice, every word was clear. As the musicians performed, our thoughts were directed inward. The program was all too brief. It was a varied program combining some Christmas songs and two beautifully performed piano works – a Sonata by Haydn and a prelude by the forward-looking Russian composer, Alexander Scriabin. I remember Joel Cohen very well as a friend and as a musician. Perhaps some of you do also when he was principal cellist of the Oakland Symphony many years ago. For some reason, Joel felt unappreciated or should I say underappreciated? He left California and moved to Vienna where he was immediately employed at the highest levels. I visited with him when I had some concerts in Vienna back in 1992. His knowledge and insight of history and religion were remarkable. This was bolstered by the ability to explain the most difficult questions with a simple sincerity. And now to discuss a very thorny problem: The great Bohemian composer Antonín Dvořák was a major influence in American music and culture while he resided in America in the early 1890s. All musicians know that Dvořák was able Antonín Dvořák to completely change the course of American music. He did so by recognizing the diverse cultural wealth that America possessed. Dvorak mobilized the entire country into action. In addition to his musical deeds, he was a perspicacious observer of social issues. One of his observations was that influential Americans were far more interested in sports than in the arts. These “powerful” people built sports arenas with the mistaken idea that they could glorify themselves. Can any of you name any of the sports personalities from the 1890s? Well… there was John L Sullivan. But just about anybody can name the famous musicians of that era. The Piedmont Post of December 17 featured a letter from Sue Malick, the Board President of the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Her letter was an appeal for support. I second her appeal and turn to the readers of the Piedmont Post for support. We must do everything we can to preserve the arts in Piedmont. Our Piedmont Center for the Arts is a true treasure and is known throughout the world. Our Piedmont Center for the Arts hosts concerts of a wide variety and extraordinary art is available to all. In addition to the concerts and the graphic arts, there are plays and numerous other cultural events. For a nominal fee, audiences can attend concerts and programs of all kinds and then attend opulent receptions. Please read Sue Malick’s letter of appeal in the Piedmont Post issue of December 17 on page 20. We need the support of City Hall. A memorial concert was performed on Sunday afternoon in St. Mary’s Cathedral in honor of cellist Joel Cohen. He was an outstanding musician and an inspiration to all of us.

articles.text: KAWS exhibition at SFMOMA The internationally renowned artist KAWS’ towering, inflatable sculpture is now overlooking downtown San Francisco, making its Bay Area debut atop the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA). The nearly 36-foot-tall inflatable sculpture “COMPANION” opened to the public last month and is currently installed on SFMOMA’s rooftop for a limited time. The installation marks the 14th stop of the global KAWS: HOLIDAY project following appearances across Australia, Europe and Asia. The free public artwork coincides with KAWS: FAMILY, the artist’s first major West Coast museum exhibition, now on view at SFMOMA through May 3, 2026. The rooftop sculpture is visible from San Francisco’s downtown core, Yerba Buena Gardens and surrounding Cultural Benefit District. “KAWS has a distinct appeal to a vast array of audiences with his iconic characters and meticulous work in a stunning range of mediums,” said Christopher Bedford, Helen and Charles Schwab Director of SFMOMA. “The playful and contemplative works, a dynamic blend of his street art practice and formal education, offer something for everyone. His large-scale public installations have wowed audiences worldwide, and his playful and poignant retrospective exhibition promises to connect museum visitors with art in entirely new ways.” Since its launch, the KAWS: Photo by Mogli Maureal HOLIDAY project has attracted more than 20 million visitors worldwide, with previous installations in cities including Hong Kong, Doha and Melbourne, according to the museum. Inside the museum, KAWS: FAMILY presents more than 100 works spanning three decades of the artist’s career. Organized by the Art Gallery of Ontario, the exhibition explores KAWS’ evolution from his early graffiti practice in Jersey City and Manhattan to a multidisciplinary career encompassing sculpture, painting, drawing, product design and large-scale public art. The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art is located at 151 Third Street in downtown San Francisco. Visit www.sfmoma. org for more information.
articles.title: KAWS’ art sculptures now on view atop SFMOMA

Enjoy complimentary refreshments with tickets from https://events.com/r/tickets/1014544, or pay $30 at the door, cash/check only. Saturday, January 17 – February 28 Printmakers Art Exhibition The California Society of Printmakers returns to Piedmont with its 111th Annual Members’ Exhibition, displaying close to 100 works of printmaking art, demonstrating the incredible variety of style and process that falls within this field. The exhibit will be open most weekends from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays; there will be an opening reception on Saturday, January 24, from 1 to 4 p.m., as well as a closing reception on February 28 from 11 a.m. to 1:30 p.m., providing good chances of meeting and learning from many of the artists, one or two of whom will also be present during the weekend open hours. The exhibition is free to visit, and the works will also be available to enjoy during your attendance at any of PCA’s public events. Saturday, January 17, 5:00 p.m. Michael Stehr Art Lecture The Impressionist movement is regarded by many as the most important revolution in Western art since the Renaissance. When the Impressionist renegades gathered in 1874 to hold their very first group exhibition outside the state-regulated parameters, many thought they were building the next revolution to upend Paris. The most compelling of these relationships was between Berthe Morisot and Édouard Manet. Join local art historian Michael Stehr as he presents a 50-minute illustrated lecture The lecture is designed to prepare attendees for the current exhibit at the Legion of Honor in San Francisco. Admission to the lecture is $20 per person, Cash only, at the door. For more info, email Michael at mstehrart@gmail.com. Saturday, January 31, 6:00 p.m. Cristiana Pegoraro Piano Concert The incomparable Italian piano master Cristiana Pegoraro returns once more to Piedmont for another recital, as always supporting her work runniing an arts academy in Narni, Italy. The President of Narnia Arts Academy and the Artistic Director of Narnia Festival, hailed by the New York Times as “an artist of the highest caliber,” Italian-born pianist Cristiana Pegoraro has performed on the world’s most prestigious stages, including Lincoln Center, Carnegie Hall, the United Nations (New York), the Sydney Opera House, Festspielhaus (Salzburg), Musikverein (Vienna), Royal College of Music (London), Auditorium Parco della Musica (Rome), and Teatro alla Scala (Milan). Ms. Pegoraro has appeared as a soloist with acclaimed orchestras and ensembles worldwide and throughout her home country of Italy. Her 2003 New York City concert took place in the presence of mayor Michael Bloomberg aboard the battleship-museum USS Intrepid. February 2026 — a month full of promise Look forward also to details about more chamber music from Benicia Chamber Players (Feb. 7, 7 PM); piano & flute duo Carl Blake & William Underwood (Feb. 8, 4 PM); gemologist Sacha Grippando discussing jewelry in the visual arts (Feb. 12, 6:30 PM); piano prodigy Richard Dowling playing both classical and ragtime music on Valentine’s Day (Feb. 14, 7:30 PM); the In the Tradition Jazz & Pop Piano Trio celebrating Valentine’s Day (Feb. 15, 4:30 PM); and chamber music from both San Francisco’s Insight Chamber Players (Feb. 21, 7 PM) and from the Berkeley Symphony and Friends Chamber Series (Roots & Resonances, Feb. 22, 4 PM)! pages.text: 20 Wednesday, December 31, 2025 Features Walking on Wednesday Walkers thank first responders and visit the Twelve Days of Christmas displays By Dick Carter It was Christmas Eve last Wednesday, and 22 walkers from the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesday group, along with one canine companion, gathered at the Exedra at their usual morning hour. The group often jokes that it never rains on Wednesday mornings in Piedmont, and once again the saying held true. The walkers were pleased to know that members of the Piedmont Police and Fire Departments would meet them later for a group photo in front of the Piedmont Firehouse. Joining the group were police officers Tyler Petit and Hugo Diaz, along with fire captain Justin McNulty, lieutenant Zach Heliker, engineer Anthony Reneria, and firefighter-paramedics Chris Kruger, Viktorya Franzen and Gary Randolph. With Christmas just hours away, the walkers reflected on the essential services provided year-round by the city’s police officers and firefighters. They expressed particular appreciation for those who serve 24 hours a day, seven days a week, including on holidays. As a small gesture of thanks, the group brought boxes of donuts from Colonial Donuts on Lakeshore Avenue, a local business that, like public safety services, is open around the clock. The group made a short walk to the Veterans Building and called the Police Department to let staff know they had something waiting outside. After these cheerful visits, the walkers regrouped at the Exedra and turned to the holiday theme of the day, the “Twelve Days of Christmas.” One member shared the history behind the English carol, explaining that it may have carried a deeper meaning. From 1558 to 1829, Roman Catholics in England were not permitted to practice their faith openly, and some believe the song was written with two layers of meaning. While it appears on the surface as a festive counting song, each gift is thought to represent a religious concept that children could remember. Inspired by the carol, the walkers set off to search for neighborhood displays created by residents along Highland, Guilford, Caperton and Sheridan avenues. On the way to Guilford Avenue, the group passed through Piedmont Park and paused to check the water flow in Bushy Dell Creek, which was running well after the recent rain. At 137 Guilford Avenue, the walkers spotted two turtle doves displayed in a front window. From there, the conversation turned to inflation and affordability, prompted by the annual PNC Christmas Price Index. For more than four decades, PNC Bank has calculated the cost of the twelve gifts in the song as a playful way to illustrate changes in consumer prices. This year, the total cost of one set of all twelve gifts was reported at $51,476.12, an increase of 4.5 percent from last year, driven largely by labor costs. As the walk continued, the group found display after display. On Highland Avenue, they admired a sparkling partridge in a pear tree, followed by windows featuring nine ladies dancing, eight maids a-milking, four calling birds and three French hens, including one set drawn by a home’s three children. Turning onto Caperton Avenue, they located five golden rings, seven swans a-swimming and six geese a-laying. Along Sheridan Avenue and back toward Highland, the remaining gifts appeared in more windows. With their holiday search complete, the walkers headed home to continue their Christmas celebrations. They did so with appreciation for the service of Piedmont’s police officers and firefighters, gratitude for neighbors who brightened the season with their window displays, and enjoyment of the simple pleasure of walking together in the community. articles.text: While walking along the block of Highland/Sheridan/Caperton, you may come across a Twelve Days of Christmas display. The block’s holiday tradition is based on the song “Twelve Days of Christmas”. Ann Lin Martinez and Christina Miller started this tradition in 2021. Since then, it has continued to evolve and change as different neighbors take over each year. Each day of Christmas is represented by a display visible from the sidewalk of a neighbor’s home. Over time, neighbors have added their own twists to evolve the tradition. Unlike the Advent calendar, which counts down to Christmas, the “Twelve Days of Christmas” start after Christmas and ends on Epiphany (when the Wise Men (Magi) visited baby Jesus). As such, the display can be seen from early December until January 5. We are grateful to the participating neighbours for setting up and maintaining the displays throughout the display period. These displays have made our block very festive and ready for Christmas. You can find the “Twelve Days of Christmas” displays on Highland Avenue, Guilford Road, Capeton Avenue, and Sheridan Avenue. articles.text: Aging is a universal journey, yet many people feel unprepared for the transitions it brings. This spring, Piedmont Adult School will offer Stages to Aging, a series designed to provide clear guidance, practical insight, and confidence as adults plan for their own aging or support loved ones. Participants will explore the five stages of aging—from self-sufficiency and interdependence to dependency, crisis management, and end-of-life planning. The series focuses on understanding available services, learning how to access resources, and making informed decisions at every stage of life. Each class meeting will feature an industry expert addressing a specific aging-related topic. The January–February and March sessions cover different subject matter, allowing participants to benefit from taking one session or both. Detailed content information is provided on the website. The course is taught by Jennise Mendoza, founder of STAGES for Life, who has worked with older adults for more than 17 years. Her background as a professional organizer, bookkeeper, legal assistant for a Social Security Disability law firm, and insurance professional gives her a well-rounded understanding of the practical and emotional challenges older adults face. Her presentations educate and empower participants as they navigate the aging process. For enrollment information, visit piedmontadultschool.org or call 594-2655. articles.text: On a Wednesday night, in December 2019 Piedmont resident Mark Herrick hosted the first neighborhood meditation group session with four or five neighbors out of the Herrick’s hous. Fast forward six years and now Herrick hosts two mediation groups every Wednesday only missing two scheduled weeks during Covid. The morning Meditation Group class started in 2022 and meets in the Piedmont Center for the Arts every Wednesday from 9-10 a.m. This group is consistently fully registered with 25 people, and Herrick is looking into opening another session in the summer of 2026. The online Zoom group still meets as well, from 7:30-8:15 p.m. every Wednesday. This group grew out of the 2019 Wednesday evening community sit, which met until the covid virus hit, then took two weeks off, before moving over to Zoom. Although Herrick initially thought doing mediation over Zoom might be weird and didn’t know if it would work, it has become increasingly popular and the group hasn’t missed a meeting since. articles.text: The Cancer League’s annual Holly Ball brought together donors and supporters for an elegant Black and White–themed gala on Friday, December 5, at the Claremont Country Club. The black-tie affair, chaired by Lisa Sauer, raised funds to support groundbreaking cancer research across the Bay Area. Sauer and her committee transformed the Club with refined décor that set the tone for the evening. Guests mingled during a lively cocktail hour, enjoying signature drinks including the Noir & Blanc and the Tuxedo, a Bulleit bourbon specialty. Following dinner, auctioneer Joe Cunningham launched the evening’s program with two exclusive live auction packages: a curated wine collection and a private tour of a UCSF research lab led by Dr. Alan Ashworth, President of UCSF’s Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center. Winners will receive a rare, behind-the-scenes look at pioneering work being done by UCSF researchers. The program’s most moving moment came with the presentation of the Cancer League’s inaugural Founders’ Award to Gary Kovacs. A cancer survivor and longtime supporter of the League’s mission, Kovacs was recognized for his commitment to advancing early-stage, high-potential cancer research. His remarks inspired attendees to give generously, raising more than $200,000 during the paddle-raise alone. Cancer League President Jenna Caldwell praised Sauer and the many volunteers whose work made the event a success. She also expressed gratitude to UCSF for its sponsorship and to CIBC Private Wealth Management for its continued corporate support. “We are grateful for the generosity of all our many sponsors and donors, both corporate and individual,” Caldwell said. “It is with all of this support that we can continue funding innovative cancer research.” Proceeds from the Holly Ball will be granted to accredited Bay Area nonprofits dedicated to fighting cancer. The Cancer League’s next fundraiser, Spring Soiree, is scheduled for April 23, 2026. To donate or learn more about the Cancer League, please visit www. thecancerleagueinc.org. articles.text: A trip to Scotland means different things to different people. Some think of Scotch; others, of bagpipes, kilts, and Braveheart. And while I endorse all four, to me the best thing about Scotland is its castles. Whether meticulously preserved or overgrown with ivy, stately or quaint, towering above the moor or hidden on an island in a loch, Scottish castles are self-contained time machines that transport you to the country’s medieval past and offer a closer look at the history of this freedom-loving nation. They make for a charming and accessible part of your Scottish itinerary, provided you’re ready to drive on the wrong side of the road. I first experienced Scottish castles thirty years ago, on a quasi-engagement trip with my future husband, when we both studied in England. We stayed in a hostel across from the magnificent royal castle of Edinburgh and explored a dozen more along the North Sea coastline. Most were damaged during Cromwell’s campaigns in Scotland, and the memory of their crumbling arches etched against the gray-blue sea stayed with me as years went by. When, this spring, our younger daughter surprised us by choosing Scotland’s University of St. Andrews for her undergraduate studies, I knew that moving her in would include some castle visits. With the help of our new companion, ChatGPT, I put together a quick itinerary that included one on a lake, one on the coast, and one near Fife, where the University is located, about 1.5 hours north of Edinburgh. ChatGPT proposes, God disposes. It so happened that a San Francisco friend was visiting Scotland at the same time and insisted that we visit Fingask Castle, home of his friends. It was just a short drive from Dundee, where we would be staying, and from St. Andrews, where the owners’ children went. A visit like this, the thinking went, would alleviate our parental anxieties about leaving the youngest child an ocean away. For someone who gets excited even by castle ruins, the prospect of visiting an inhabited castle with its own Wikipedia page felt rather exhilarating. The morning after our arrival from London, we scratched our AI itinerary, piled into a large rental Mercedes, and set off to explore the foothills of the Scottish Highlands between Rait and Perth. It is important to mention that Scotland has not only the highest concentration of castles, but also the highest number of roundabouts in the UK and quite possibly the world, which makes for an intense driving experience given that roundabout entry rules are different, the roads are narrow by American standards, and have no road markings. The traffic direction feels wrong—you’re driving on the left while sitting on the right, which creates a sense of charging into a non-stop head-on collision (the big left-pointing arrows attached to the windshield of our rental helped identify other terrified non-Scottish drivers but not much else). By the time we got off the freeway, which felt more like a two-lane street with big-rigs, we were so worked up that we missed a giant TO CASTLE sign and drove for a few miles through fields and farmland, eventually ending at a farmhouse as misleadingly suggested by Google Maps. The morning after our arrival from London, we scratched our AI itinerary, piled into a large rental Mercedes, and set off to explore the foothills of the Scottish Highlands between Rait and Perth. It is important to mention that Scotland has not only the highest concentration of castles, but also the highest number of roundabouts in the UK and quite possibly the world, which makes for an intense driving experience given that roundabout entry rules are different, the roads are narrow by American standards, and have no road markings. The traffic direction feels wrong—you’re driving on the left while sitting on the right, which creates a sense of charging into a non-stop head-on collision (the big left-pointing arrows attached to the windshield of our rental helped identify other terrified non-Scottish drivers but not much else). By the time we got off the freeway, which felt more like a two-lane street with big-rigs, we were so worked up that we missed a giant TO CASTLE sign and drove for a few miles through fields and farmland, eventually ending at a farmhouse as misleadingly suggested by Google Maps. After returning to the village Topiary garden at Fingask Castle and Gardens and now traveling uphill where the sign was pointing, through some charming woods, past hidden lakes and meadows, we arrived at what certainly could be a castle: when I rang the doorbell, as the invitation email suggested, the sound produced was that of an average church bell. No one came, leaving us to survey the weathered walls of uneven gray stones that had an undeniable medieval feel. In a couple of minutes, a car pulled over, and from it emerged a gray-haired gentleman in a white shirt and slacks, whom we correctly guessed to be Andrew Threipland, the castle’s owner. A trio of Springer spaniels, all of the same brown and white coloring—a mother, a daughter, and a granddaughter, as we later learned—rushed to greet us, filling the fresh autumn air with sharp barking. As we followed Andrew around the corner, past a lawn so vast and impeccable it could easily be mistaken for a city park, Fingask finally revealed itself: a formidable three-storied manor, its wings added and reshaped over centuries, with the roof edged in crow-stepped gables rising in a jagged line against the clear sky. Ahead, in the stone-paved courtyard brightened by flag garlands, a small fountain sparkled in the sun, and a rustic table was set up for brunch. Soon we were hugging Andrew’s wife and our hostess, the effervescent Helen Molchanoff, whose Russian roots served as a faint connecting line between us. The lands of Fingask appear in early medieval charters and were associated with the Bruce family, whose line would later produce Robert the Bruce, the king who secured Scotland’s independence. In the early 17th century, the estate passed to the Threiplands, who became its enduring custodians. Although they lost the property for a time after backing the unsuccessful Jacobite uprisings to restore the House of Stuart, the family later repurchased it. Today Fingask remains their home, spread over 240 picturesque acres in the hills between Perth and Dundee. Carefully restored and lovingly maintained, it brings together unique historic structures, orchards, tree-lined walks, and sweeping vistas, along with an eclectic array of medieval and Renaissance artifacts; the Mary Queen of Scots sundial graces an entryway, for instance. It even has its own small loch, a tranquil place visited by swans. Fingask is also home to a surrealist topiary garden, a whimsical stretch of clipped yews and hollies shaped into domes, swirls, and spirals. It sits between the main house and the wedding pavilion, a modern white structure capable of accommodating 300 guests beneath its central dome. (The Threiplands host some twenty-five weddings per year). One of the most striking features of the pavilion is an antique fourhorse town carriage that resides on its front lawn; gleaming yellow, with large, spoked wheels, it looks like a prop from a Disney princess movie, though nobody ever saw it turning into a pumpkin. articles.text: Piedmont Flix Fest continues on January 8 One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what the Piedmont Flix Fest, which meets on the second Thursday of each month, offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting, and then a lively discussion of it afterward. The Flix Fest’s January feature is the spirited 1992 comedy, My Cousin Vinny, directed by Jonathan Lynn and starring Joe Pesci and Marisa Tomei, who won a Best Supporting Actress Academy Award for her witty performance. The film centers on New York lawyer Vinny Gambini, who has never won a case. When his teenage cousin Bill and his friend Stan are accused of murder in a backwater Alabama town, it’s up to Vinny to save him from jail, even though he’s only ever tried personal injury cases before, and lost all of them. Marissa Tomei plays his wide-eyed financée, Mona Lisa Vito, who travels south with him. My Cousin Vinny was a critical and financial success. It will be screened on January 8th at 1:00 p.m. The showing takes place in the Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors will open at 12:45. The movie is free and available to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration is encouraged and can be done at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunch The next movie in the Piedmont series is the Bill Murray comedy, Lost in Translation, to be shown on February 12.

articles.text: T he Pied mont Sen iors recently visited one of the Bay Area’s quiet architectural gems: the Marin County Civic Center in San Rafael. What they encountered was not just a government building, but a place where daring architecture, film history and legendary music intersect. Designed by Frank Lloyd Wright, the Civic Center was his last and largest public project — and a controversial one from the moment he was selected in 1957. At the time, critics questioned whether Wright’s bold vision belonged in a county government complex. Construction began in 1960, shortly after Wright’s death, and the finished design proved to be far ahead of its time, embracing a distinctly futuristic aesthetic decades before such ideas became mainstream. Long, low-slung buildings sweep across the hills, joined by a soaring rotunda and unified by Wright’s unmistakable palette of pink stucco, blue rooflines and scalloped balconies. The result feels more like a forward-looking civic campus than a traditional seat of government. The complex has since earned widespread recognition for that ambition. It is designated both a National Historic Landmark and a California Historical Landmark, honors that underscore its architectural and cultural significance. During the visit, the seniors toured the Board of Supervisors meeting room and the library nestled within the central rotunda, learning that The Piedmont Seniors pose at the entrance to Joe’s of San Rafael, where they enjoyed a scrumptious and filling lunch. Pictured are (L to R): Yorkman Lowe, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Edith Hereso, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, Nancy Hinsch, Sue Getreuer, Jim Ayotte, Gloria Wilmer, and Greg Jurin. portions of the chamber seating were constructed decades ago by inmates at nearby San Quentin. Indoors, light-filled spaces, thriving plants and artwork by local residents soften the building’s grand scale and reflect Wright’s belief that public spaces should feel humane and accessible. The Civic Center’s influence extends well beyond architecture. Its striking design has made it a sought-after filming location, appearing in George Lucas’ first feature-length film, THX 1138, later in the Star Wars prequel trilogy, and in Gattaca, where it stood in for a sleek vision of the future. Musicians have also left their mark: Peter Frampton recorded parts of Frampton Comes Alive there, and the Grateful Dead recorded their album In the Dark in the Veterans Memorial Auditorium. After the tour, the group continued on to downtown San Rafael for a traditional Italian lunch at Joe’s of San Rafael, a longtime local favorite. The outing offered a reminder that some of the region’s most remarkable history, architectural, cinematic and musical, can be found just beyond the freeway, hiding in plain sight. articles.text: Ho! Ho! Ho! The Piedmont Seniors spent a recent afternoon celebrating the holiday season with a scrumptious luncheon at the Claremont Country Club. Once everyone finished their last bite of a delectable tiramisu dessert certificates of appreciation were given to a few group members who contributed to the Piedmont Seniors throughout the year, including Carole Jones, Gloria Wilmer, and Lily Guardia-Labar. The group then participated in a joyous gift exchange. It was the perfect ending to a merry holiday get-together. If you would like to find out more information about the Piedmont Seniors program, contact Janet Epstein, coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: This year brought no shortage of uncertainty, both globally and right here in our local communities. Political tension, economic unpredictability, and fluctuating interest rates created a complex backdrop for the real estate market. Yet despite the noise, real estate in 2025 continued to demonstrate its remarkable resilience, especially in Piedmont and the surrounding East Bay neighborhoods where community, lifestyle, and location remain strong pillars of value. While national news cycles often tell a dramatic story, the local experience tends to look different—and more stable. Families are still moving for schools, lifestyle upgrades, more space, and proximity to the people and places that matter most. Even in a year shaped by shifting headlines, these core motivations remained unchanged. Interest rates stayed at the forefront of nearly every real estate conversation. After several rounds of movement, many buyers adopted a cautious waitand-see approach. Others recalibrated what affordability looked like for them and moved forward with intention, focusing on longterm value rather than short-term fluctuations. Sellers, on the other hand, discovered that today’s market rewards thoughtful preparation more than ever. Strategic pricing, curated presentation, and meaningful improvements became crucial components of a successful sale. In many segments of the market, the pattern of effortless bidding wars has shifted, replaced by a more measured and informed pace— though standout homes still draw strong interest. One of the most influential shifts has been the continued rise of remote and hybrid work. More professionals now have the flexibility to work from anywhere, and they’re redefining what “home” means. This shift has increased demand for houses with dedicated office spaces, multi-functional rooms, and outdoor areas that enhance everyday living. It has also expanded the search radius for many buyers who no longer need to be within commuting distance of an office five days a week. As a result, secondary markets, suburban neighborhoods, and lifestyle-focused communities have experienced increased activity. Political and economic unrest played their part as well, influencing how people made decisions around one of their most significant investments. But instead of halting movement, the uncertainty seemed to spark a renewed appreciation for the stability that real estate continues to offer. Even in unpredictable times, real estate remains a tangible, long-term asset—something that provides both security and a foundation for future growth. Families are still buying. Sellers are still selling. Investors are still investing. What has changed is the level of intention behind those choices. As we look toward the remainder of the year and beyond, one thing is increasingly clear: real estate remains deeply connected to the way we live, work, and envision our futures. In a year defined by ongoing change, the ability to adapt— to market conditions, lifestyle needs, and personal goals—has become our greatest strength. And as always, our local market continues to demonstrate its capacity to evolve with the times. Thinking about your next move in 2025? By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama, I got a text that I did not recognize saying, “Hey, do you want to go out for dinner tonight?” I was about to answer it, but my daughter said just to delete it. She said it was probably a scam. How do I know if something is legitimate or not? –Sheila, Oakland Dear Sheila, Your daughter is correct. This was very likely a phishing attempt. If someone you know sends you a text, their name will usually appear because they are already in your contacts. A message from an unknown number, especially one that jumps straight into an invitation or request, is a strong warning sign. Scams have become harder to spot, particularly with the rise of artificial intelligence. Several publications, including AARP Magazine, have highlighted common scams circulating this year. Here are a few to watch out for. One long-running scam is the tech-support scam. You may receive a phone call, email or pop-up window claiming your computer has a virus. The message may warn you not to close the window or shut down your computer, sometimes accompanied by loud or alarming sounds. You are given a phone number to call, and a “helpful” person insists they need remote access to your computer. Once inside, they point to ordinary system files and claim they are dangerous, then offer costly protection plans. If you provide payment information, charges can escalate quickly. Another increasingly common scam involves fake credit card decline notices. In this case, shoppers may be on a fraudulent website or have clicked a bad link and are told their card was declined. They try another card, which is also “declined,” even as charges quietly accumulate on both accounts. A newer and particularly harmful scam is known as “pig butchering.” A scammer contacts a victim through a dating app, social media or a text claiming to be looking for an old friend. Over time, they build trust through friendly or romantic conversations. Once trust is established, they introduce a supposed cryptocurrency investment and direct the victim to a fake website. When the victim tries to withdraw funds, excuses follow, and eventually the scammer disappears. There are clear red flags to watch for: unsolicited messages, pressure to act quickly, promises of high returns, reluctance to meet by video, or requests to move conversations to apps like WhatsApp or Telegram. With AI, scammers can even mimic the voices of friends or relatives using audio pulled from social media, inventing emergencies that demand immediate money. To protect yourself, never use debit cards online. Credit cards offer far stronger fraud protections. If you receive a call claiming to be from a relative in trouble, verify it by contacting that person directly. Do not click links sent by text, email or social media. At home, I have thick albums of newspaper clippings that track my daughters’ milestones, the high moments of tennis tournaments, poetry slams, and graduation speeches. I also love seeing neighbors and friends (and, occasionally, my own family) in the “Where in the World Are We?”, the wildly popular column where residents pose with the paper on their travels. “It’s about connection,” Gray says. “About people recognizing themselves and each other in these pages.” Gray’s commitment to Piedmont didn’t stop at the newsroom; it carried into nearly every corner of the city’s cultural and civic life. In 2011, he became one of the founding members of what would become the Piedmont Center for the Arts (PCA), a project he viewed as a natural extension of the Post’s mission to uphold the town’s cultural and civic vibrancy. Over the fourteen years since its founding, PCA has hosted everything from chamber music to student recitals, providing a stage not only for visiting performers but for Piedmont’s own artists, writers, and musicians—including Cathrall himself, a devoted musician who occasionally takes the piano bench with his jazz ensemble, Shades of Gray. Among his contributions to PCA is launching the Berkeley Symphony’s Chamber Series. As PCA president Sue Malick recalls, “Gray was instrumental in forming the relationship with Berkeley Symphony’s René Mandel that brought all of their chamber concerts to the Center, where he has remained one of the series’ chief sponsors.” His commitment to Piedmont’s young people has been equally steady. In recognition of his decades of service, Cathrall was named Grand Marshal of Piedmont’s Fourth of July Parade in 2024—a fitting tribute to a man whose tireless commitment to his city has helped bring the community together. Having built a model of sustainable local journalism and enhanced the vibrancy of the local art scene, Gray has recently tapped Misha Edel, a former journalist and a longtime Piedmont resident, as the Post’s new Executive Editor. Edel will work closely with Gray on setting the paper’s editorial calendar and coverage priorities and will also focus on growing subscriptions and advertising revenue, streamlining operations, and developing a digital edition that complements the print paper. “The paper has always belonged to Piedmont,” Gray says. “Our job is to make sure it keeps serving this town for generations to come.” While Edel takes the helm of day-to-day publishing, Gray will turn more of his attention to philanthropy, a new chapter that he promises to unveil at his milestone birthday celebration in February 2026. Yet even as his focus widens, his imprint will remain on every page—the headlines, the stories, and the civic pride they reflect. As he looks ahead, Cathrall remains what he’s always been: the steady presence at the center of Piedmont’s civic life, an engaged and truly compassionate public servant whom many town residents consider a dear friend. The Post he built continues to bind us together—and to prove that when a community believes in local journalism, its spirit thrives. Nearly three decades later, the Post endures as Gray envisioned it: an honest, lively reflection of the town it serves. articles.text: As Dylan gains creative control, his music begins to rise to mainstream attention, writing songs about the growing political and social unrest at the time. This resonated with listeners, especially Joan Baez (Monica Barbaro). The two would become close friends and eventually go on tour together. Through his tour with Baez and playing at large festivals, Dylan became a cultural icon, but with the newfound fame comes increasing frustration with the expectations of both the music industry and the folk community. His lack of creative freedom frustrates Dylan, and he lashes out, taking his music in a new direction that frustrates the folk community. The climax comes during his performance at the 1965 Newport Folk Festival. I won’t reveal what happens at the festival, but it encapsulates how Bob Dylan lived his life. A man fighting not to conform to everyone’s expectations of who he should be but pushing to be the artist that he desired and write songs about topics he cared about. A Complete Unknown delivers a fantastic representation of Bob Dylan from Chalamet, in one of his best films. The movie leaves audiences with the message of individuality. A Complete Unknown. Directed by James Mangold. Starring Timothée Chalamet, Elle Fanning, Edward Norton, and Monica Barbaro. Duration 2 hr. 21 min. Rated R. Released 2024. Genre: Docudrama, music. Streaming on Hulu, Disney+, and fuboTV.

articles.text: For more than a century, Piedmont Church has been a church of open doors - welcoming and affirming all who wish to gather, worship and serve. This history of acceptance provides a powerful atmosphere where our faith in God, combined with the love for our neighbor, creates the perfect ‘church home’ for many. Some say they attend Piedmont Church to rest, to find shelter from many of life’s challenges. Others find spiritual strength by participating in worship, preparing them for the week ahead. Those who enjoy serving their community explore ways to give back through our local and international Mission Partners. And, fellowship brings vivid life to it all. For the many reasons we give thanks during this season, we are most grateful for our church and for you - the friends we’ve known, and those we’ve yet to meet.
